# Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit below this line.

`const self = this` is a way to reach the outer `this` from a `function` callback, which has a `this` of its own. An arrow function does not, so inside it `this` is still the outer one. With an arrow function you do not need the extra variable, and nobody can mix up `self` and `this`.

This rule is on by default in TypeScript files.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad */}
```ts
class Timer {
  seconds = 0;

  start() {
    const self = this;
    setInterval(function () {
      self.seconds++;
    }, 1000);
  }
}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```ts
class Timer {
  seconds = 0;

  start() {
    setInterval(() => {
      this.seconds++;
    }, 1000);
  }
}
```

## Options

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allowDestructuring` | `true` | Allow taking properties out of `this`: `const { seconds } = this`. |
| `allowedNames` | `[]` | Names of variables that may hold `this`. |

Reported with `allowDestructuring: false`:

{/* bad {"options": [{"allowDestructuring": false}]} */}
```ts
class Timer {
  seconds = 0;

  report() {
    const { seconds } = this;
    return `${seconds}s`;
  }
}
```

With `allowedNames: ["self"]`, only `that` is reported:

{/* bad {"options": [{"allowedNames": ["self"]}], "count": 1} */}
```ts
class Timer {
  start() {
    const self = this;
    const that = this;
    return [self, that];
  }
}
```
